title: Layered neutrals: how to keep a beige room from going flat
author: Preet Ahluwalia
authorBio: Preet has led the group's interiors practice since 2012 and still reviews every material board that leaves the Mumbai studio.
excerpt: Three tones, two textures and one honest material. A working method for neutral rooms that still hold your attention after a year.

body.text: Every second brief we receive asks for a neutral palette, and roughly half of those rooms end up looking tired within a year. The problem is almost never the colour. It is that the room was built from one tone repeated across five different finishes, so nothing catches light differently.
Pick three tones and hold the line

We work to a simple ratio on site: a dominant wall tone, a mid tone for joinery, and a deeper grounding tone for floors or a single heavy element. Anything beyond three reads as indecision once the furniture arrives.
A neutral room survives on texture, not on colour. If you can close your eyes and still describe the surfaces, it will hold.

body.caption: Handleless oak cabinetry in a Bandra kitchen — matte fronts against a honed stone counter.

body.text: Let one material be unmistakably real

Stone with visible movement, unfilled travertine, solid teak with a rift-sawn grain — one genuine material anchors the whole scheme and gives the eye somewhere to land. Everything else can be a sensible engineered substitute and nobody will notice.
The corollary matters too: do not put two loud naturals in one sightline. A veined marble island under a burled veneer ceiling is two arguments happening at once.
Plan the light before the finishes

Neutral schemes live or die on colour temperature. We specify 2700K in living areas, 3000K in kitchens and utility, and we test both against the actual samples on site before the ceiling is closed. Repainting is cheap; rewiring a false ceiling is not.

title: The storage audit we run before designing any kitchen
author: Meera Iyer
authorBio: Meera runs the design studio in Mumbai and has detailed more than four hundred kitchens across the west coast.
excerpt: Before a single elevation is drawn, we count what actually has to live in the room. It changes the drawing every time.

body.text: Indian kitchens carry more than the modular catalogues assume: bulk grain, pressure cookers, a second set of festival utensils, and at least one appliance that arrived as a wedding gift and cannot be discarded.
Count it, do not estimate it

Our audit is a one-page list filled in with the client at their current home. Tall items, wet items, daily items, seasonal items. We photograph the existing cabinets with the doors open, which is usually the most useful drawing in the whole set.
Clients rarely ask for more storage. They ask for storage that does not require kneeling.
Drawers over shutters, almost always
Below counter level we specify drawers by default. The cost premium is roughly eleven per cent on the base units and it removes the single most common complaint we hear at the one-year service visit.

body.caption: Adjacent living room in the same apartment — the kitchen palette carried through in a quieter register.

body.text: Above counter level we go the other way: shutters that stay shut, one open bay for the things used every day, and nothing decorative on display that has to be dusted weekly.

title: Designing rooms where the technology disappears
author: Raghu Menon
authorBio: Raghu leads the electronics business and its service network across eleven cities.
excerpt: How our two companies plan cabling, speakers and screens before the first wall is drawn, rather than after handover.

body.text: The most expensive thing in a home automation project is usually the chasing and making good that happens because nobody knew where the equipment would sit.
One coordination meeting, held early

Because the interiors and electronics teams sit inside the same group, we hold a single joint meeting at concept stage. Screen sizes, speaker positions, rack location and cooling, and the route for every cable are fixed before the joinery drawings are released.
If you can see the technology from the doorway, we have detailed it badly.

body.caption: Fluted walnut panelling with a flush screen recess and concealed speaker fabric.

body.text: Where the rack goes
Racks belong in a ventilated utility cupboard with a service door, never inside a sealed TV unit. We allow 400mm of clear depth and a dedicated circuit, and we label every termination at both ends.
Design for the person who services it
Somebody will open this in three years, and it will not be the person who installed it. Accessible terminations and a printed schematic taped inside the door cost nothing and save an afternoon.

title: What a good appliance service call actually looks like
author: Farah Qureshi
authorRole: Head of Service, Fabluxe Home Solutions
authorBio: Farah built the group's service desk and its 48-hour response commitment across eleven cities.
excerpt: Response time is the number everyone quotes. First-visit resolution is the number that decides whether a client buys from you again.

body.text: Our service desk tracks two figures. Time to first visit, which most brands publish, and first-visit resolution, which most do not.
Carry the part, not the promise

Engineers travel with a stocked kit for the twenty most common failures across the ranges we sell. It ties up working capital and it is the single reason our first-visit resolution sits above eighty per cent.
A second visit is not a service call. It is an apology with a travel cost attached.
Close the loop in writing
Every call ends with a short written note: what failed, what was replaced, and what the client should watch for. It is also how we spot a bad batch three weeks before the manufacturer tells us.

title: Switching the joinery shop to certified timber
author: Devika Rao
authorBio: Devika joined in 2021 to run the group's material and waste programmes across both companies.
excerpt: Ninety-one per cent of our panel volume is now certified. The remaining nine per cent is the interesting part of the story.

body.text: We started the switch in 2023 expecting the obstacle to be price. It was not. The obstacle was supply consistency in the sizes our shop actually cuts.
The cost was smaller than the rescheduling
Certified panels landed roughly six per cent above our previous board, absorbed inside our material contingency. The real cost was two projects rescheduled while we waited on a shipment.

body.caption: Certified stock in the Vasai joinery shop, stickered and acclimatising before machining.

body.text: Chain of custody paperwork is only worth anything if the shop floor can read it at the saw.
What is left
The remaining volume is specialist veneer for restoration work where certified stock in the right species does not exist. We publish that number rather than round it away.

title: Putting solar on four showroom roofs, and what it returned
author: Devika Rao
authorBio: Devika joined in 2021 to run the group's material and waste programmes across both companies.
excerpt: 412 kW installed across four roofs, covering 38% of retail load. The payback maths, without the marketing rounding.

body.text: Showrooms are unusually good solar candidates: heavy daytime load from lighting and cooling, flat roofs, and a landlord relationship that lasts long enough to justify the capital.
The numbers

412 kW across Mumbai, Pune, Surat and Bengaluru. In the first full year the arrays covered thirty-eight per cent of retail electricity load, against the forty-four per cent our consultant modelled. Monsoon months underperformed the model considerably.
Every solar model we were shown assumed a clean panel. Ours are cleaned fortnightly and still lose output to coastal grime.
What we would do differently
Specify monitoring at the string level from day one. Our first two installations report at the inverter only, which means an underperforming string can hide for a quarter.

title: Fabluxora opens a design studio in Bengaluru
author: Fabluxe Group
authorBio: Announcements and updates from the group's communications desk in Mumbai.
excerpt: A 4,200 sq ft studio and material library in Indiranagar, our first permanent design presence outside Maharashtra.

body.text: Fabluxora Interiors has opened a design studio and material library in Indiranagar, Bengaluru. The space houses fourteen designers, a full sample library, and a client review room with mock-up walls.

body.caption: The new Indiranagar studio, with the sample library along the north wall.

body.text: Why Bengaluru, and why now
We have delivered in the city since 2019 from Mumbai, and the travel was starting to show up in our snag numbers. A resident team shortens every review cycle.
You cannot detail a room properly from an airport lounge.
The studio is open to clients by appointment from June, and the sample library is available to external architects working with us on live projects.

title: Twenty-four apprentices join the joinery programme
author: Fabluxe Group
authorBio: Announcements and updates from the group's communications desk in Mumbai.
excerpt: Our fourth intake at the Vasai workshop, with a paid eighteen-month structure and a hiring commitment at the end of it.

body.text: Twenty-four apprentices have joined the Fabluxe joinery programme at Vasai, the largest intake since the scheme began in 2022.
How the programme runs
Eighteen months, paid throughout, rotating across machining, assembly, finishing and site installation. Each apprentice is paired with a senior craftsperson who carries no more than three at a time.

body.caption: Bench training at Vasai — the first six weeks are hand tools only.

body.text: We hire from the programme first. Of the sixty-one who have completed it, forty-nine are still with us.
Applications for the 2027 intake open in January and are advertised through the ITI network in Palghar and Thane districts.
